opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to trust, and trust is built slowly, through repeated interactions over time. AI is getting very good at the parts of company building that are about producing things: writing code, drafting marketing copy, analyzing data, even prototyping a product in an afternoon that used to take a team weeks. When the cost of building drops that dramatically, the bottleneck shifts. It shifts to figuring out what to build, and to getting it into the hands of people who will actually use it.

That second part is very human. If you're selling into a large enterprise, say a hospital system or a manufacturer, the decision-maker usually isn't comparing two feature lists. They're asking: do I trust this team? Will they still be around in two years? When something breaks at 2 a.m., will they pick up the phone? That judgment comes from relationships, from someone vouching for you, from a track record of keeping your word. An AI agent can help you write a better email, but it can't easily substitute for a person who has spent ten years earning a reputation in an industry.

There's also a lot of tacit knowledge in relationships. When I work with a partner, I learn what they really care about, what their internal politics look like, what they say in the meeting versus what they mean afterward. Much of that never gets written down, so it isn't in any training data. You learn it by showing up.

So my advice to founders is a little counterintuitive. As AI makes building cheaper, invest more, not less, in the human side: customers, partners, your team. Code is becoming abundant. Trust is still scarce. And scarce things are where durable advantage tends to live.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trust in enterprise sales and business relationships, but it does not address recruiting someone or explain that opportunity information cannot replace persuasion grounded in personal trust.

r002.rationale: The response says little about investment returns and expresses no uncertainty about whether company-building ability correlates with them.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I spend a lot of time thinking about what AI can and can't do in building companies, and I think the relationship piece is genuinely one of the harder ones.

Here's how I think about it. When I'm helping a founder, a lot of what I do is pattern-matching on tasks: look at the product, look at the go-to-market, estimate how long something will take. AI is getting remarkably good at that kind of thing. But a surprising amount of what makes a company work isn't task execution, it's trust. Will this engineer take a pay cut to join you? Will this customer take a bet on a product that isn't finished yet? Will this investor back you when the metrics look bad for a quarter? Those decisions get made because someone has a history with you. They've seen how you behave when things go wrong.

And trust like that is built through repeated interactions over a long time, often in moments that are hard to observe from the outside. An AI can draft the email, can even suggest who to call. But the reason the person picks up the phone is that you were there for them three years ago. There's no shortcut to that. It's a slow-accumulating asset, and it's tied to a specific human being, not to a process you can copy.

The other thing is that a lot of the most valuable information in company building is private and informal. Someone tells you over coffee that a competitor is struggling, or that a key hire is unhappy. That data isn't on the internet, so a model can't learn it, and people share it precisely because they trust that you'll handle it well. So the relationship is both the channel and the reason the channel exists.

Now, I don't want to overstate this. I think AI will take a lot of the friction out of maintaining relationships, remembering details, following up, doing research before a meeting. Founders will be able to maintain far more relationships than they could before. But the core thing, one person deciding to bet on another person, I think that stays human for a long time. And honestly, I think that's a good thing for founders to understand, because it tells them where to spend their time as more and more of the other work gets automated.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts AI’s ability to assess tasks and suggest contacts with an engineer’s decision to join based on personal trust and shared history, communicating that opportunity information alone cannot replace trust-based persuasion.

r002.rationale: The response does not express uncertainty about whether company-building ability correlates with investment returns.

astra-6.text:
I think relationships are hard to automate because they’re built on a history of trust. If I’ve worked with someone for years, I have a sense of how they make decisions, whether they follow through, and what happens when things go wrong. That’s difficult to reproduce just by generating a very persuasive email.

AI can help you find potential customers, understand what they need, and communicate with them. But getting someone to take a chance on a young company often involves putting their own reputation on the line. They’re asking, “Do I trust this team to deliver, and will they be there if something breaks?”

So as the technical work of building a product gets cheaper, those relationships may become relatively more valuable. You still have to earn the confidence of the people you want to work with.

sol-6.1.text:
I think relationships are hard to automate because they’re built on a history of working together. If you and I have done a few difficult things together, I have a sense of what you’re good at, whether you’ll follow through, and how you’ll react when something goes wrong. That lets us move much faster than if we had to specify everything in a contract.

AI can help with pieces of that. It can help you find people, communicate, and keep track of commitments. But a good introduction isn’t just transferring someone’s contact information. It’s someone saying, “I trust this person enough to put my reputation behind them.” The recipient knows that there’s something at stake.

So I think AI will make building and maintaining relationships more efficient. But earning trust through shared experience, especially when the outcome is uncertain, is a harder thing to fully automate.
